To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inactivation of the parietal region of macaque monkey brain, the PRR, produces the hallmarks of optic ataxia, misreaching but not mis-saccading for visual targets.

inactivation of the parietal region in which neurons are preferentially active during reach preparation causes misreaches to visual targets but not mis-saccades, and reach errors are larger for the preferred targets of the neurons in this region.
inactivation of the parietal region of the brain called parietal reach area (PRR) causes a human-like optic ataxia in monkeys and that this is due to a disruption of reach goals in the PRR.

the PRR is a key node of the reach system and that the PRR lesion is a neural basis of the OA syndrome in humans.

The main takeaway from our work is that

we show that a specific region of the monkey brain is involved in reaching for objects in the visual field, but not in making saccadic eye movements, and that inactivating this brain region can produce the same symptoms in monkeys that are seen in humans with a specific neurological disease, called optic ataxia.
we can now use optogenetic inactivation to causally link specific brain regions to specific behaviors.
